From https://mathstodon.xyz/@jonmsterling/116246709451263085:

I am also not too impressed by the existence of second-party checkers in the context of a language that lacks decidable type checking. Because something has to give, these checkers will be (necessarily) incomplete in one way or another, most likely each in different ways. This is because lean’s failure of completeness of conversion almost certainly manifests in heuristic ways that are not predictable or replicable…

For a fail safe checker to provide confidence, it needs to be complete. This is not possible with Lean’s core language as designed, and it will not be possible for Lean itself until they find new leadership.

From https://mathstodon.xyz/@jonmsterling/116246762960668025:

The de bruijn criterion remains a very good idea for systems that are decidable, or undecidable systems that produce full derivations. The latter is not practical for a full type theory, so nobody does it. So in practice, de bruijn is useful only for decidable systems. Not Lean.

From https://mathstodon.xyz/@jonmsterling/116246739335249500:

@RanaldClouston It is deterministic as far as I know. The issue is that if you are implementing a checker for a broken/incomplete system, there are a million different places where you can put the incompleteness, because syntactic invariants are like squeezing a balloon. When one is broken, you can sometimes make it hold but then another thing breaks. Because there is so much room for movement here, it becomes very difficult to even specify what it would mean to have an independent checker. Even if this is fully specified, which would be possible to do, the result would be of limited value in my opinion.
Can anyone elaborate on Lean's undecidable type checking? What does that mean?

My understanding is that "type checking is undecidable" means it is not possible to write a terminating algorithm that determines for all possible t : Exprs whether they are of type T : Expr. Arguably all you need to know is that the algorithm is correct when it says "t is of type T", and that on the ts you care about, it terminates.

For a fail safe checker to provide confidence, it needs to be complete.

Is this true? Can someone create a variant of Lean that is complete? How hard is it to do so?

@Mario Carneiro has proved that it is not decidable. But that does not stop perfect safety. What is guaranteed is that each type-checker will reject some correct terms because of failing to prove equality, hence that types are correct.

From my experience with working for a while on porting trepplein (unfortuantely not finished) one thing that is true is that the small trusted kernel in Lean is not that small (as the post says the kernels are a few thousand lines) and is fairly complex. It is straigtforward to write an independent kernel for first-order logic say and straightforward to see by eye that it is correct. But this is not saying there is any fundamental limitation (and so far as I understand there is none).
it is possible to make a typechecker that is complete but doesn't necessarily terminate on bad inputs
(the most obvious naive algorithm is enumerating typing derivations)
In practice do the typecheckers start like this but limit resources to timeout?

My interpretation of Jon Sterling's comments is that there is some idealized type theory of Lean, in which there is a set T of well-typed expressions. But the set T is undecidable (however it may be recursively enumerable/semidecidable as per Mario Carneiro's comment above). So the standard implementation of Lean only accepts a subset S₁ ⊂ T of statements as well typed, and S₁ is decidable. Since S₁ ≠ T, we say that the standard implementation of Lean is incomplete. An external type checker for Lean, say nanoda, would accept a subset S₂ ⊂ T. Sterling's concern is that we might have S₁ ≠ S₂, which could limit the value of external checkers. A potential solution would be to standardize on a decidable subset S₀ ⊂ T that all type checkers would implement exactly, but Sterling claims this is hard and of limited value, "because syntactic invariants are like squeezing a balloon". I believe Meven Lennon-Bertrand's message basically states that in spite of this, we do in fact already have S₁ = S₂ for all existing external kernels, so S₀ essentially already exists.
yeah, it's not really an issue, this set does exist

On a non-technical note, I wish comments about foundations of math and proof assistants were more careful to separate positive and normative claims (in the same sense of positive and normative economics).

I asked Jon what he meant . To summarise his words, if your type theory is not complete, then there are two ways you can build external checkers. One is for all of them to accept the exact same subset of terms, in which case they may not be truly independent external checkers, because they have to reproduce the type checking of the core kernel exactly for every term. The other is that each external checker is independent and potentially accepts a different subset of terms and then you don't have a consensus on which external checker to trust when there is a disagreement (this is what @Niels Voss is also saying I believe).
What Meven is saying is that external checkers currently adopt the first approach, which might mean that they are not truly independent in some sense of that word
What is their working definition of "independent"? That seems to be load bearing here.

I think a working definition would be "You read the spec of the type theory, and write your own type checker for it without consulting existing type checkers". This is still an inadequate definition since writing type checkers for dependent types is a skill known to a small community and they would probably share a lot of ideas.

One thing I find interesting is situations like batteries#1601, which changed something in a library that would have otherwise been fine except for its interaction with infrastructure related to external checkers. I think it would be fair to say this is an example of a subtle interdependency?

I won't push this too far since I don't want you to have to

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I think a working definition would be "You read the spec of the type theory, and write your own type checker for it without consulting existing type checkers". This is still an inadequate definition since writing type checkers for dependent types is a skill known to a small community and they would probably share a lot of ideas.

A cleanroom implementation would be cool, but it doesn't seem very realistic in that (1) the intersection of people with the background knowledge, time, and desire to do this is vanishingly small (empirically empty so far), and (2) I don't know that there's a lot of room for creativity if you also expect your checker to work with a large corpus like mathlib. Some of the implementation details that are effectively necessary are not going to appear in a description of the type theory. I think this is probably true of all of the DTT based provers, though maybe this is realistic for something like metamath or HOL light.

I won't push this too far since I don't expect you to respond on their behalf (I was just curious whether they'd given any more information in your side conversation) but that definition of independence doesn't necessarily comport with the assertion that decidability is the fundamental issue undermining independence and the utility of external checkers (see "I am also not too impressed by the existence of second-party checkers in the context of a language that lacks decidable type checking" and "For a fail safe checker to provide confidence, it needs to be complete").

The thread does not (to me) adequately explain what the connection is, and the replies devolve into ancillary claims about issues with the type theory.

I am not the right person to answer that. The definition of "independent" was an adhoc one I created in the absence of a concrete definition anywhere. As I also point out, this definition faces the issue of the community of typechecker authors being a small and closely connected one.
Someone did ask the relevant question https://mathstodon.xyz/@shiranai/116249258412257583

Chris Bailey said:

(2) I don't know that there's a lot of room for creativity if you also expect your checker to work with a large corpus like mathlib. Some of the implementation details that are effectively necessary are not going to appear in a description of the type theory. I think this is probably true of all of the DTT based provers, though maybe this is realistic for something like metamath or HOL light.

Suppose the theory is bare Martin Lof type theory with no extra features, then for conversion (defeq) checking alone there are multiple options: Normalization by evaluation (typed and untyped variants), Reduction based conversion, hereditary substitution, etc. These all give exactly the same results (as long as the implementation is correct, which is the point).

I don't know what you're referring to by implementation details, but (1) typeclass resolution and elaboration is not handled by these independent checkers usually, and a lot of engineering effort of mathlib is on those; (2) the mechanism of when to unfold definitions etc should only affect the efficiency, not the result of typechecking. Efficiency is somewhat of an issue for extremely large library like mathlib, so maybe it blocks some really slow but simple (and so easy to verify) algorithm to be used.

Trebor Huang said:

I don't know what you're referring to by implementation details, [...]. Efficiency is somewhat of an issue for extremely large library like mathlib, so maybe it blocks some really slow but simple (and so easy to verify) algorithm to be used.

I mean things like reduction heuristics (when/where to reduce, and how aggressively), some of the caching and approximate solution checking (I think this is the technical term for short-circuiting) in the kernel's lazy delta reduction code, and implementation choices for things like free variables; there was recently an instance in which an auxiliary proof for Char.isUpper created just the right set of circumstances during reduction to type check efficiently when a separate local context was used to track free variables from let expressions, but blew the stack if a totally separate local context was not used (in a way that is logically equivalent, but led to slightly different reduction pathways, and this was not necessarily a lean-specific construction).

A big part of this is the workload created by users. Users are going to write code with the sole criteria that it checks in some acceptable amount of time using the official version, where the official version will have made some set of implementation decisions and optimizations. As the big important code bases in an ecosystem get larger and/or the code gets more extreme, the reliance on that set of choices and optimizations just gets stronger over time, such that any deviation means those changes in efficiency are very difficult to recover from. Whether they're logically equivalent, or whether one solution is extremely simple or elegant is out the window if it's not going to finish checking in any meaningful amount of time or will OOM any consumer hardware it runs on.

I suspect that for any nontrivial ecosystem, there's less flexibility in practice than one would hope due to this user-created workload issue. The artificial benchmarks in the sort of mini-survey conducted by Andras Kovacs in the smalltt readme are an interesting data point; naive substitution with lots of caching is very good at instantly handling approximate/short-circuiting conversion obligations; NbE is not. Users of those systems are going to introduce code reliant on that into their projects, which means an NbE based checker is eventually going to run into problems. On the flip side, NbE can be much faster at pure reduction, so users of those systems are likely to introduce a lot of code which relies on reduction that would crush a naive substitution implementation.

None of this is tied to decidability.

It may or may not be the case that Lean's type theory puts it in categorically worse position on this dimension relative to comparable systems, I'm not sufficiently knowledgeable about the implementation details of any other DTT systems (I suspect this is not the case, but I don't think any comparable systems have secondary checkers, so it's hard to say).

Chris Bailey said:

As the big important code bases in an ecosystem get larger and/or the code gets more extreme, the reliance on that set of choices and optimizations just gets stronger over time, such that any deviation means those changes in efficiency are very difficult to recover from.

I would say this is just an argument to stop relying on heuristic optimizations, but rather develop systems with nice and predictable properties. For example, the controlled unfolding mechanism has strict theoretical guarantees of when a definition unfolds, and isn't sensitive to conversion checking strategies. This is already implemented in Agda, but until large codebases start to extensively use this feature, it's hard to say whether it works in practice.
Judging purely from the number of threads on zulip, a lot of the definition unfolding issues/workarounds are about how it interacts with elaboration, instead of kernel checking (although there are some). Maybe somebody should actually keep count.

Chris Bailey said:

naive substitution with lots of caching is very good at instantly handling approximate/short-circuiting conversion obligations; NbE is not.

Can you point to the place where it says so in smalltt? At a quick glance I couldn't locate it.

The table and annotations for the raw conversion checking section of the README. It's also just apparent from the way closures and substitution work; with closures you generally need to quote in order to get something that can reasonably be compared for equality quickly or cached (and overuse of quotation back into syntax to do this yields a worse version of substitution), while you pretty much always have that with substitution (and which you then pay for over the course of reduction).

Chris Bailey said:

I suspect that for any nontrivial ecosystem, there's less flexibility in practice than one would hope due to this user-created workload issue.

Wait, but this simply argues it's difficult (or impossible) to achieve truly independent implementations of the kernel. What's the relation of this to what Jon's claiming, precisely? He is saying that decidability of languages is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for second-party checkers to provide confidence.

I made a comment about the degree of independence one could realistically expect, because someone referenced Meven Lennon-Bertrand's comments about independence. You replied to it and we went from there.

What decidability, in practice, has to do with the trustworthiness of a type checker's results or the validity of the deBruijn criterion in general has not really been addressed, here or there.

Chris Bailey said:

What decidability, in practice, has to do with the trustworthiness of a type checker's results or the validity of the deBruijn criterion in general has not really been addressed, here or there.

The point was that if a term is accepted by independent typechecker A but rejected by independent typechecker B, you don't know which typechecker to trust: A could be wrongly implemented and mistakenly accepting a bad term/false proof, while B could be [ADDENDUM: correctly implemented and] rejecting a correct proof due to incompleteness. This undermines the "multiple independent typechecker ==> greater safety" argument, not the small kernel criterion.

Josh Chen said:

Chris Bailey said:

What decidability, in practice, has to do with the trustworthiness of a type checker's results or the validity of the deBruijn criterion in general has not really been addressed, here or there.

The point was that if a term is accepted by independent typechecker A but rejected by independent typechecker B, you don't know which typechecker to trust: A could be wrongly implemented and mistakenly accepting a bad term/false proof, while B could be rejecting a correct proof due to incompleteness. This undermines the "multiple independent typechecker ==> greater safety" argument, not the small kernel criterion.

why does it undermine that? This is assuming in the case you are ellucidating you trust the proof if one typechecker fails, but why would you do that? If one typechecker fails you investigate why, and if it's due to incompleteness you can massage your proof term so that it works. If all typecheckers accept it, there is greater trust/safety, I think that remains valid.

Determining if a failing typecheck is "due to incompleteness" amounts to deciding if the typecheck-failing term you're seeing does in fact have a typing derivation, so we're back to the same issue as in my previous message.

If all typecheckers accept a term, it calls into question the independence of the typechecking algorithms used (again, due to undecidability of typechecking you'd expect "independent-where-it-matters" typecheckers to accept/reject different problems), and therefore of the independence of the occurrence of bugs in the entire cohort.

Josh Chen said:

If all typecheckers accept a term, it calls into question the independence of the typechecking algorithms used

If they all accept any term? A specific term?

It would be interesting to do something like coverage-guided fuzzing to see when you could get divergent behavior from different type checkers, but I'm not sure what undecidability has to do with this since I'd also expect decidable algorithms to have terms for which type checking doesn't terminate in a practical amount of time.

@Josh Chen I think it would help us to have an explanation of the design space for typecheckers for CIC. Specifically, what sort of variations can we expect from multiple independent type checkers? Only some of us come from PL background and even there, I believe writing dependent type checkers is a specialized niche skill.

Josh Chen said:

Determining if a failing typecheck is "due to incompleteness" amounts to deciding if the typecheck-failing term you're seeing does in fact have a typing derivation, so we're back to the same issue as in my previous message.

Right, but I'm not talking about a general decision procedure, I'm talking about a concrete person looking at it. Guiding the typechecker by adding more intermediate steps that typecheck easily should solve most of these practical instances, and assuming that if you can't do that you have less trust sounds reasonable too. In both cases I don't see this as a fundamental problem.

Josh Chen said:

If all typecheckers accept a term, it calls into question the independence of the typechecking algorithms used (again, due to undecidability of typechecking you'd expect "independent-where-it-matters" typecheckers to accept/reject different problems), and therefore of the independence of the occurrence of bugs in the entire cohort.

Why? There is some intrinsic assumption here that independence would be meaningful in a way that I don't see at least why it has to be in theory

Josh Chen said:

The point was that if a term is accepted by independent typechecker A but rejected by independent typechecker B, you don't know which typechecker to trust: A could be wrongly implemented and mistakenly accepting a bad term/false proof, while B could be rejecting a correct proof due to incompleteness. This undermines the "multiple independent typechecker ==> greater safety" argument, not the small kernel criterion.

This situation where verifier A says an environment is OK, verifier B says it is not, is possible in any system. I don't think there's any property of a given formal system (including decidability) that would allow the tool to just say "this type checker is correct in this csae and this one is not, for X reason".

Josh Chen said:

If all typecheckers accept a term, it calls into question the independence of the typechecking algorithms used (again, due to undecidability of typechecking you'd expect "independent-where-it-matters" typecheckers to accept/reject different problems), and therefore of the independence of the occurrence of bugs in the entire cohort.

If undecidability is a property of the theory, and typecheckers are necessarily expected to implement the theory regardless of how cleanroom they are, I don't understand how you would reasonably expect to observe differences here between properly implemented typecheckers.

More broadly, I think there's a misunderstanding about what kind of additional safety is being claimed by proponents of external checkers. My understanding of the intent behind soliciting multiple typecheckers is to guard against implementation bugs (across the checker's whole dependency graph) and compilation bugs. This is a very concrete thing; users have the option to run different typecheckers on a code base and see whether all of the lights are green. If they're not, one has the option to manually investigate what's happening inside the checker and observe the behavior to determine what's causing divergent behavior.
